6.97: So, one is receiving the electrons from NADH, complex II is receiving the electrons from FADH, and then they are both handing them off to CoQ10 or ubiquinone. 6.98: One last comment on this is that as the electrons are moving through these complexes, in order to maintain this static equilibrium with all these negative charges, the cells are also pumping out positively charged molecules in the form of protons. So protons, bound to a hydrogen atom, actually—these hydrogen protons are getting pumped out. This matters in the end. There are four protons that are getting pumped out at complex I, none getting pumped at complex II, two getting pumped out at complex III, and then finally, four getting pumped out at complex IV. 6.99: If it started with NADH coming to complex I, then you had the four at I, the two at III, and the four at IV, resulting in ten protons that were pumped out. That will matter in a minute. Now we only have the two coming out at III, and then the four coming out at IV. So, we are left with only six having been pumped out in that instance. So, we had ten pumped out or six pumped out, and that matters because all of those electrical charges are starting to get irritated by being so close to each other.
6.100: And they're sitting in that what's called an intermembrane space. All of this what's been happening has been happening on the inner mitochondrial membrane. If you put them too close to each other, you're going to get some static. Something's going to happen. So, they start pushing against each other.
6.101: Before the cell can take advantage of this, the last and final note to mention about the electron transport system is oxygen. Oxygen has been waiting and waiting to eat an electron. 6.102: This is how—oxygen is called the final electron acceptor and it is able to accept those electrons without becoming a reactive oxygen species or a superoxide radical, a very damaging molecule that we've talked about in the Q&A earlier.
